Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Game Info 1.1 Currencies 1.2 Terminology used in the game 1.3 Auto-advance (Hammer) 2 Taking Your Turn 2.1 Taking an additional action 3 Game End 4 Tiebreaker 5 Rebellion Expansion 6 Titan Module 6.1 Starting dice 6.2 Titan board 6.3 Ancient shards and extra cards 7 Goddess Module Game Info Dice Forge is a game about rolling your dice to collect resources. You can spend those resources to upgrade your dice, or perform Heroic Feats (purchase cards) that give you points and special powers. Currencies Gold - Yellow - Used to upgrade your dice or to activate some reinforcements.. Sun Shards - Orange - Used to perform Heroic Feats (purchase cards) and take extra actions. Moon Shards - Purple - Used to perform Heroic Feats (purchase cards). Glory Points (GP) - Green - Contributes directly to your score; can be earned by rolling the appropriate dice face, activating certain reinforcements, and at the end of the game the Glory value of all collected cards is added to your score. Terminology used in the game Divine Blessing - The act of rolling both your dice and receiving the rolled resources. Minor Blessing - Rolling a single die and receiving the rolled resources. Reinforcements - After rolling their dice, the active player may use any special powers gained from purchased cards. Auto-advance (Hammer) If you have purchased The Blacksmith's Hammer card and enable the "Auto-advancement" button, Gold earned from any source will be applied to the Hammer. If "Auto-advancement" is disabled, you will be prompted to allocate Gold earned to either the Hammer or your inventory. Taking Your Turn On each player's turn, all players roll their dice and collect the rolled resources. (In a two-player game, players roll their dice twice before each player's turn.) You are then allowed to perform one action: Forge - Spend Gold to upgrade your dice. You can purchase any number of new die faces, but each face you buy must be unique. (Your dice may have duplicated sides, but the faces you purchase within a given Forge action must be different.) Heroic Feat - Spend Sun and/or Moon Shards to purchase a single card. Place your Hero pawn on the pedestal containing the card you wish to purchase. If another player's pawn was on that pedestal, they receive a Divine Blessing and are returned to the central island. (This is known as " Ousting " their hero.) Taking an additional action Finally, the active player may spend two Sun Shards to take a second action if they wish; if they choose to take a second Heroic Feat action, they can perform the same or a different Heroic Feat. Game End You play 10 rounds with 3 players, and 9 rounds with 2 or 4 players. Much like in real life, the player with the most Glory Points at the end of the game wins. Tiebreaker If enabled, the following tiebreakers are implemented: Number of die faces forged. Number of Heroic Feats accomplished. Number of remaining resources. The player having started the game the earliest. Rebellion Expansion You have two different modules available to play. Will you join forces with the Titans in the titan module, or undertake Hera's labyrinth and take home even more treasure than ever before in the Goddess module? You can play with either one of the two types and each one plays very differently to each other. In addition to different modules, you can also choose just to use the new heroic feat cards and leave the modules out. This gives the base game a lot more variety. Gold is basically worthless after a couple turns and if someone doesn't explain that at the get go, you're toast. [Rating: 1/10] This game has such a cool premise - but by the time you have upgraded your dice to be awesome... the game is over. Have only played at two, but the game arc was rubbish. Spend the first few turns doing the easy stuff, finally get some cool faces on the dice, then the game is over before you get to do the cool stuff.

[Rating: 1/10] [b]A dice-building gimmick in search of meaningful decisions.[/b] Physically replacing die faces is undeniably clever and initially delightful, but the strategic layer surrounding that novelty is astonishingly thin. Most turns offer obvious purchases, little meaningful interaction, and progression so straightforward that the game rarely rewards exploration beyond identifying the efficient upgrade path. A remarkable component innovation attached to one of the least demanding decision spaces in modern board gaming.

[Rating: 1/10] The customizable dice are really cool but the game built around them is lame and uninspired.

[Rating: 1/10] Lavish art and the dice look nice.   – You upgrade a pair of dice and then hopefully resources to exchange for points.  None of the steps created particularly interesting decision points – Low interaction and too long for me, 15-20 mins would be better for this lightweight style game x You may never roll your upgraded die faces.  This is my biggest beef with dice builders, unlike a deck builder you might never experience your upgrades which is very unsatisfying.  Really need lots of dice rolls to balance this which you don't get (there were 9 rounds of rolling a pair of dice).

[Rating: 1/10] The game when things happen to you and you have virtually no agency. A little better than Monopoly  because it's shorter.

[Rating: 1/10] I do not enjoy this game. The theme of build your own dice was a fun mechanic until you realize the plastic used to create the dice are not evenly distributed. They are basically weighted to one side and when you find that side this game breaks. Your chances are BS and adding to your engine is not as fun when the interaction between players is very low.  Also once your behind your out of the game and the rolling just continues.

[Rating: 2/10] A nightmare. I hope you will be Lucky when playing this game. You can improve your dice, if you have no luck in the firstgame turns and your oppponents have nice rolls, you have no way to come back in the party. NO interrest.

[Rating: 2/10] Have played it at a friend's house 3 times.   1st time - Woah, this is a cool game! 2nd time - Ok, this seemed exactly like the first game. 3rd time - Oh, Dice Forge again. Yipeee...  The "strategy" involved is extremely light, and it is apparent after playing the game two times what the best cards are that you need to get to win.   With kids, it might be fun to play with. But, if you enjoy strategy and replayability, I'd take a pass on this one.
